**VERDICT: REVISE** **Overall Assessment**: The component uses correct semantic HTML (`

The `h1` → `h3` skip, followed by an `h3` → `h2` jump later, creates a fragmented information architecture that screen readers cannot reliably navigate. Contrast ratios pass WCAG AA, and no interactive patterns require ARIA, but the structural gap must be fixed before shipping. **Pre-commitment Predictions**: Before reading code, I predicted: (1) heading hierarchy breaks due to skipped levels, (2) missing page-level context if rendered standalone, (3) potential contrast issues with `#666` text on white, and (4) lack of skip navigation/landmark structure for full-page use. Investigation confirmed predictions 1 and 2 as active design gaps; prediction 3 was resolved by measured contrast ratios; prediction 4 is context-dependent but flagged as an enhancement. **Critical Findings** (blocks access): *None.* The component does not block core functionality or trap users, but it contains a MAJOR structural gap that degrades assistive technology navigation. **Major Findings** (significantly degrades experience): 1. **Skipped heading levels break the document outline** - Evidence: `src/components/BlogPost.tsx:6` (`

    Why Accessibility Matters

    `) immediately follows `

    ` on line 4. Later, `src/components/BlogPost.tsx:21` (`

    Tools and Resources

    `) appears after an `

    ` on line 17. - User group impacted: Screen reader users, cognitive accessibility users - WCAG/APG citation: WCAG 1.3.1 (Info and Relationships) — "Information and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text." Heading hierarchy defines programmatic structure. - Expected behavior: Headings must follow a logical, sequential outline (`h1` → `h2` → `h3`). Screen readers use this outline to build navigation menus and convey section depth. - Actual behavior: Outline jumps `h1` → `h3`, then later `h3` → `h2`. This fragments the document tree, causing screen reader heading outlines to appear disjointed or nested incorrectly. - Confidence: HIGH - Why this matters: Screen reader users rely on heading outlines to scan content structure. Skipped levels force them to manually read through sections to understand hierarchy, defeating the purpose of semantic headings. - Fix: Change the first four `

    ` and the first `

    ` to establish a proper parent-child relationship. Ensure all subsequent headings follow sequential nesting rules. **Minor Findings** (friction but workaround exists): - **Contrast ratios pass AA but use low-saturation color for body text**: `color: #666` on white background yields ~5.74:1, which passes WCAG 2.2 AA normal text requirements (≥4.5:1). No action required, but note that reducing contrast further will fail. **Enhancements** (best practice not met): - **Missing page-level context if rendered as a full page**: If this component is used as a standalone blog post page, it lacks `
    ` landmark wrapping and skip navigation. If used as a reusable card/widget, the heading hierarchy should be documented as relative to its parent container. Add `lang` attribute context if multilingual support is planned. - **Visual-only section separation**: Sections rely solely on margins for visual distinction. Consider adding `aria-labelledby` or explicit landmark roles if this component will be embedded in complex layouts where programmatic section boundaries are needed. **What's Missing** (gaps, unhandled edge cases, unstated assumptions): - Logical heading sequence: The document outline is fragmented. Screen reader navigation menus will show disjointed sections. - Page-level navigation context: No skip link or `
    ` landmark if this represents a full page. Keyboard users lack a quick path to main content. - Component usage documentation: It's unclear whether this is a full-page template or a reusable card. Heading levels should be scoped to the component's intended insertion point. **Multi-Perspective Notes**: | Perspective | Alarm Level | Trigger Signal | |-------------|-------------|----------------| | Screen reader | HIGH | Broken heading outline prevents programmatic navigation | | Keyboard-only | LOW | No interactive elements; focus management not applicable | | Low vision | MEDIUM | Contrast passes, but low-saturation text (`#666`) may struggle in high-contrast mode or with magnification if reduced further | | Cognitive | HIGH | Skipped headings disrupt information architecture and scanning patterns | | Vestibular & motion | LOW | No animations or motion | | Auditory access | LOW | No media elements | | Environmental contrast | MEDIUM | `#666` passes AA but sits near the threshold; verify in forced-colors mode | - **Screen reader user**: Will hear "Introduction to Web Accessibility, heading level 1" then immediately "Why Accessibility Matters, heading level 3". The outline tool will show a broken tree. Navigation is fragmented. - **Keyboard-only user**: No interactive elements present. Tab order is N/A. If embedded in a page with links/buttons, focus management depends on parent layout. - **Low vision user (200% zoom, high contrast)**: Layout reflows correctly at 800px max-width. Focus indicators are N/A here. Contrast passes AA but `#666` may lose distinction in Windows High Contrast mode if system themes override colors. Verify with UA forced-colors toggle. - **Cognitive accessibility**: Heading hierarchy is a core cognitive scaffold. Skipping levels forces users to infer structure visually, increasing cognitive load. Sequential headings reduce scanning effort. **Verdict Justification**: The component passes semantic HTML checks and avoids ARIA misuse, but the heading hierarchy violation is a MAJOR design gap that directly impacts assistive technology navigation. It does not block access entirely (hence not CRITICAL), but it significantly degrades the experience for screen reader and cognitive users by breaking the programmatic document outline. The component must be revised to establish a sequential heading structure before acceptance. If this is intended as a reusable card, heading levels should be adjusted to `h2`/`h3` relative to its parent, or documented clearly. **Open Questions (unscored)**: - Is this component intended to render as a full page or as a reusable card/widget? This determines whether `
    ` and skip navigation are required at the parent level. - Will this component be embedded in layouts where multiple instances exist on one page? If so, duplicate `h1` elements will violate WCAG 1.3.1; each instance should use `h2` as its top-level heading. - Are there dynamic states (loading, error, success) planned for this component? If so, aria-live regions and aria-busy handling will need to be designed.
